title: I Let the Model-Yacht Pond Clock Catch the Skipper Who Took My Numbered Hull

parts.text: I stepped into the pond dock at 9:05 a.m. and skipper Ned was already using numbered gear. The board said: ONE HULL. SIXTY MINUTES. SAILS STAY WITH THE SLOT. I was thirty-four, pond secretary, holding a clipboard that listed our numbered hull. Ned shrugged. "Skippers are the pond." I photographed the board, the booking, and his leftover keel on my numbered hull. Then I asked for the hull log. At 9:13 the dock pinged why Ned's name was on my keel. I kept my voice indoor and let the timestamp talk. A paper policy is only paper until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The dock can see Ned's leftover keel on my numbered hull.

social.video_title: He took my numbered model-yacht hull on my slot — Part 1/2
social.description: Pond dock, leftover keel, a sixty-minute clock he posted. I logged the hull. Would you have asked for the hull log?

parts.text: Ned called it trim until the dock asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the board, and the keel still. The hull went back to my numbered slot. Ned ran a slot of his own and told the next skipper atmosphere was always about optics. Optics is a word people use when a booking exists. Policy now has a second line: SKIPPERS ARE NOT THE POND. I keep my hull on a labeled cradle. Ned brown-bags his trim. The pond finally looks like a slot, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.description: Hull log, numbered hull, and a second line on the board. Was trim ever my keel?
